claim: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases use a variety of mechanisms to ensure fidelity of the genetic code and ultimately select the correct amino acids to be used in protein synthesis.
source: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases use a variety of mechanisms to ensure fidelity of the genetic code and ultimately select the correct amino acids to be used in protein synthesis.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in molecular biology supported by extensive literature on aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.

claim: In Escherichia coli, a non-coded amino acid produced through oxidative damage is a significant threat to the accuracy of protein synthesis.
source: We show that in Escherichia coli, a non-coded amino acid produced through oxidative damage is a significant threat to the accuracy of protein synthesis and must be cleared by phenylalanine-tRNA synthetase in order to prevent cellular toxicity caused by mis-synthesized proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing growth inhibition and m-Tyr accumulation in editing-deficient strains.

claim: m-Tyr must be cleared by phenylalanine-tRNA synthetase in order to prevent cellular toxicity caused by mis-synthesized proteins in E. coli.
source: We show that in Escherichia coli, a non-coded amino acid produced through oxidative damage is a significant threat to the accuracy of protein synthesis and must be cleared by phenylalanine-tRNA synthetase in order to prevent cellular toxicity caused by mis-synthesized proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays showing that editing-deficient strains are sensitive to m-Tyr.

claim: The accuracy of translation depends on the precise pairing of mRNA codons with their cognate aminoacyl-tRNAs during ribosomal protein synthesis.
source: The accuracy of translation depends on the precise pairing of mRNA codons with their cognate aminoacyl-tRNAs, containing the corresponding anticodons, during ribosomal protein synthesis (Zaher and Green, 2009; Rodnina, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on translation fidelity.

claim: Cognate amino acids are attached to their respective tRNAs by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.
source: Cognate amino acids are attached to their respective tRNAs by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (aaRSs), and the ability of these enzymes to distinguish between cognate and non-cognate substrates is a major determinant of the fidelity of the genetic code.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of molecular biology.

claim: The ability of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases to distinguish between cognate and non-cognate substrates is a major determinant of the fidelity of the genetic code.
source: Cognate amino acids are attached to their respective tRNAs by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (aaRSs), and the ability of these enzymes to distinguish between cognate and non-cognate substrates is a major determinant of the fidelity of the genetic code.
evidence: This is supported by general knowledge of translation fidelity mechanisms.

claim: AaRSs discriminate against near- and non-cognate tRNAs at levels compatible with typical translation error rates (∼10−4).
source: AaRSs discriminate against near- and non-cognate tRNAs at levels compatible with typical translation error rates (∼10−4) due to the structural complexity and diversity observed between tRNA isoacceptors.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of translation error rates.

claim: AaRSs can less successfully discriminate against near-cognate amino acids, which may differ from the cognate substrate by as little as a single methyl or hydroxyl group.
source: AaRSs can less successfully discriminate against near-cognate amino acids, which may differ from the cognate substrate by as little as a single methyl or hydroxyl group.
evidence: This is a well-known challenge in aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase specificity.

claim: Phenylalanine tRNA synthetase (PheRS) edits mischarged Tyr-tRNAPhe at a hydrolytic editing site ∼30 Å from the synthetic active site.
source: For example, phenylalanine tRNA synthetase (PheRS) edits mischarged Tyr-tRNAPhe at a hydrolytic editing site ∼30 Å from the synthetic active site (Roy et al., 2004; Kotik-Kogan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Mischarged Tyr-tRNAPhe is readily delivered to the ribosome by EF-Tu where it can efficiently decode Phe codons as Tyr in the growing polypeptide chain, resulting in mistranslation.
source: PheRS editing provides a key checkpoint in quality control, as mischarged Tyr-tRNAPhe is readily delivered to the ribosome by EF-Tu where it can efficiently decode Phe codons as Tyr in the growing polypeptide chain, resulting in mistranslation (Ling et al., 2007b, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: AaRS editing pathways are not conserved.
source: Despite their role in accurately translating the genetic code, aaRS editing pathways are not conserved, and their activities have varying effects on cell viability (Bacher et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2006; Bacher and Schimmel, 2007; Bacher et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations showing variability in editing across organisms.

claim: Mycoplasma mobile tolerates relatively high error rates during translation and lacks PheRS editing function.
source: Mycoplasma mobile, for example, tolerates relatively high error rates during translation and lacks PheRS editing function, as do other aaRSs in this organism (Li et al., 2011; Yadavalli and Ibba, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Mycoplasma mobile.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae cytoplasmic PheRS has a low Phe/Tyr specificity and is capable of editing.
source: Saccharomyces cerevisiae cytoplasmic PheRS (ScctPheRS) has a low Phe/Tyr specificity and is capable of editing, whereas the yeast mitochondrial enzyme (ScmtPheRS) completely lacks an editing domain, and instead relies on high Phe/Tyr specificity.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of yeast PheRS.

claim: Yeast mitochondrial PheRS completely lacks an editing domain and instead relies on high Phe/Tyr specificity.
source: Saccharomyces cerevisiae cytoplasmic PheRS (ScctPheRS) has a low Phe/Tyr specificity and is capable of editing, whereas the yeast mitochondrial enzyme (ScmtPheRS) completely lacks an editing domain, and instead relies on high Phe/Tyr specificity.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of yeast mitochondrial PheRS.

claim: Escherichia coli PheRS displays a high degree of Phe/Tyr specificity and robust editing activity.
source: Escherichia coli, in contrast, has retained both features and displays a high degree of Phe/Tyr specificity and robust editing activity (Reynolds et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Editing by PheRS and other aaRSs is not essential for viability in yeast or E. coli under standard laboratory conditions.
source: Furthermore, given that editing by PheRS and other aaRSs is not essential for viability in yeast or E. coli, it is clear that the true roles of these quality control pathways remain to be fully elucidated (Reynolds et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation and experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: AaRSs are able to edit tRNAs misacylated with a range of amino acids not found in the genetic code such as homocysteine, norleucine, α-aminobutyrate and meta-tyrosine (m-Tyr).
source: AaRSs are able to edit tRNAs misacylated with a range of amino acids not found in the genetic code such as homocysteine, norleucine, α-aminobutyrate and meta-tyrosine (m-Tyr), although the physiological relevance of these activities is unknown (reviewed in Yadavalli and Ibba, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a review citation.

claim: Both E. coli and Thermus thermophilus PheRS have been shown to edit m-Tyr.
source: Both E. coli and Thermus thermophilus PheRS have been shown to edit m-Tyr, a metabolic byproduct formed by oxidation of phenylalanine following metal-catalyzed formation of hydroxyl radical species (Huggins et al., 1993; Stadtman and Levine, 2003; Klipcan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: m-Tyr is a metabolic byproduct formed by oxidation of phenylalanine following metal-catalyzed formation of hydroxyl radical species.
source: Both E. coli and Thermus thermophilus PheRS have been shown to edit m-Tyr, a metabolic byproduct formed by oxidation of phenylalanine following metal-catalyzed formation of hydroxyl radical species (Huggins et al., 1993; Stadtman and Levine, 2003; Klipcan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on oxidative damage.

claim: Certain species of fescue grasses (Festuca spp.) produce m-Tyr as a natural defense agent that appears in the proteomes of neighboring plants.
source: Certain species of fescue grasses (Festuca spp.) produce m-Tyr as a natural defense agent that appears in the proteomes of neighboring plants, and m-Tyr accumulation in the proteome of Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells has been proposed to have a cytotoxic effect on translation (Gurer-Orhan et al., 2006; Bertin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on fescue grasses.

claim: m-Tyr accumulation in the proteome of Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells has been proposed to have a cytotoxic effect on translation.
source: Certain species of fescue grasses (Festuca spp.) produce m-Tyr as a natural defense agent that appears in the proteomes of neighboring plants, and m-Tyr accumulation in the proteome of Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells has been proposed to have a cytotoxic effect on translation (Gurer-Orhan et al., 2006; Bertin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on CHO cells.

claim: Bacterial PheRS is able to efficiently edit m-Tyr-tRNAPhe.
source: Here we show that bacterial PheRS is able to efficiently edit m-Tyr-tRNAPhe, and that this editing activity is essential for cellular growth and survival under both cytotoxic amino acid and oxidative stress conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro editing assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: PheRS editing activity is essential for cellular growth and survival under both cytotoxic amino acid and oxidative stress conditions.
source: Here we show that bacterial PheRS is able to efficiently edit m-Tyr-tRNAPhe, and that this editing activity is essential for cellular growth and survival under both cytotoxic amino acid and oxidative stress conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays under m-Tyr and oxidative stress conditions.

claim: PheRS editing in yeast provides only limited protection from m-Tyr.
source: Additionally, we show that PheRS editing in yeast provides only limited protection from m-Tyr, but instead is essential for protecting the cell from para-Tyr-tRNAPhe accumulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by yeast growth assays showing sensitivity to m-Tyr even in wild-type strains.

claim: PheRS editing in yeast is essential for protecting the cell from para-Tyr-tRNAPhe accumulation.
source: Additionally, we show that PheRS editing in yeast provides only limited protection from m-Tyr, but instead is essential for protecting the cell from para-Tyr-tRNAPhe accumulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by yeast growth assays showing editing-deficient strains are sensitive to p-Tyr.

claim: The G318W mutation in E. coli PheRS reduces posttransfer editing activity by more than 70-fold in vitro.
source: Changes to residue βG318 hinder access to the editing site and thereby reduce EcPheRS posttransfer editing activity by more than 70-fold in vitro (Roy et al., 2004; Ling et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies.

claim: Only the E. coli strain encoding wild type PheRS retained post-transfer editing activity against p-Tyr-tRNAPhe.
source: Only the strain encoding wild type PheRS retained post–transfer editing activity against p-Tyr-tRNAPhe (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the editing assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: E. coli strains with wild type pheT and pheT(G318W) alleles showed identical levels of aminoacylation activity and growth at 37°C.
source: Both strains showed identical levels of aminoacylation activity and growth at 37°C, indicating that the proofreading pathway is not required for growth under normal laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of growth and enzyme activity.

claim: The proofreading pathway is not required for E. coli growth under normal laboratory conditions.
source: Both strains showed identical levels of aminoacylation activity and growth at 37°C, indicating that the proofreading pathway is not required for growth under normal laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that editing-deficient strains grow normally under standard conditions.

claim: The D243A mutation in S. cerevisiae FRS1 eliminated p-Tyr-tRNAPhe editing in vivo.
source: Introduction in FRS1 of a mutation encoding the amino acid replacement D243A eliminated p-Tyr-tRNAPhe editing in vivo (Figure 1B; Reynolds et al., 2010) and had no effect on growth compared to wild type under standard conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the editing assay shown in Figure 1B and cited work.

claim: The D243A mutation in S. cerevisiae FRS1 had no effect on growth compared to wild type under standard conditions.
source: Introduction in FRS1 of a mutation encoding the amino acid replacement D243A eliminated p-Tyr-tRNAPhe editing in vivo (Figure 1B; Reynolds et al., 2010) and had no effect on growth compared to wild type under standard conditions.
evidence: This is based on experimental growth observations.

claim: Phenotypic microarrays revealed no significant changes in growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) compared to wild type under 1920 growth conditions.
source: Phenotypic microarrays (Biolog) were used to compare the growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) to wild type under 1920 growth conditions, and no significant changes were observed in the absence of PheRS editing.
evidence: This is based on experimental phenotypic microarray data.

claim: Elevated concentrations of p-Tyr (>3 mM) did not affect the growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) compared to wild type.
source: Elevated concentrations of p-Tyr (>3 mM) did not affect the growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) compared to wild type (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth assay shown in Figure 2A.

claim: E. coli pheT(G318W) contained similar intracellular concentrations of p-Tyr and Phe as the wild type strain.
source: Analysis of amino acid pools extracted from representative cells showed E. coli pheT(G318W) contained similar intracellular concentrations of p-Tyr and Phe as the wild type strain, indicating the pheT mutation has no effect on amino acid uptake (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by amino acid pool measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: The pheT mutation has no effect on amino acid uptake in E. coli.
source: Analysis of amino acid pools extracted from representative cells showed E. coli pheT(G318W) contained similar intracellular concentrations of p-Tyr and Phe as the wild type strain, indicating the pheT mutation has no effect on amino acid uptake (Table 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that intracellular amino acid concentrations are similar between strains.

claim: Growth of E. coli strain pheT(G318W) was inhibited in the presence of elevated intracellular concentrations of m-Tyr.
source: Relative to wild type, growth of E. coli strain pheT(G318W) was inhibited in the presence of elevated intracellular concentrations of m-Tyr suggesting PheRS proofreading activity is needed to clear mischarged m-Tyr-tRNAPhe in vivo (Table 1; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: PheRS proofreading activity is needed to clear mischarged m-Tyr-tRNAPhe in vivo.
source: Relative to wild type, growth of E. coli strain pheT(G318W) was inhibited in the presence of elevated intracellular concentrations of m-Tyr suggesting PheRS proofreading activity is needed to clear mischarged m-Tyr-tRNAPhe in vivo (Table 1; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the growth inhibition of editing-deficient strains in the presence of m-Tyr.

claim: Post-transfer editing of m-Tyr-tRNAPhe by PheRS is ablated by the G318W mutation.
source: Editing assays performed in vitro confirmed that, as with p-Tyr, post–transfer editing of m-Tyr-tRNAPhe by PheRS is ablated by the G318W mutation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro editing assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inhibitory effect of m-Tyr on growth in the absence of editing was also observed in E. coli mutants derived from strain MG1655.
source: The inhibitory effect of m-Tyr on growth in the absence of editing was also observed in E. coli mutants derived from strain MG1655 that, unlike the NP37 background, encodes an intact stringent response (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays in the MG1655 background shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Neither o-Tyr nor L-DOPA inhibited growth of wild type or the pheT(G318W) mutant E. coli strain.
source: Growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) was also evaluated in the presence of ortho-tyrosine (o-Tyr) and 3,4-dihydroxy-L-phenylalanine (L-DOPA), oxidation products of Phe and p-Tyr, respectively (Maskos et al., 1992). Neither of these non-proteinogenic amino acids inhibited growth of wild type or the pheT(G318W) mutant E. coli strain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The editing deficient frs1-1 (D243A) yeast strain showed a pronounced defect in p-Tyr resistance.
source: While the editing deficient frs1-1 (D243A) yeast strain displayed no difference to wild type under heat shock or ethanol stress, it showed a pronounced defect in p-Tyr resistance. At elevated p-Tyr concentrations, growth of the frs1-1 (D243A) strain was restricted compared to wild type (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The growth of both wild type and frs1-1 (D243A) yeast strains was comparably inhibited by addition of m-Tyr.
source: while the growth of both strains was more comparably inhibited by addition of m-Tyr (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Wild type EcPheRS did not stably charge tRNAPhe with either m- or p-Tyr.
source: Wild type EcPheRS did not stably charge tRNAPhe with either m- or p-Tyr, while G318W utilized both isomers for aminoacylation, with m-tyr being a more efficient substrate (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation assays shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: G318W EcPheRS utilized both m-Tyr and p-Tyr for aminoacylation, with m-Tyr being a more efficient substrate.
source: Wild type EcPheRS did not stably charge tRNAPhe with either m- or p-Tyr, while G318W utilized both isomers for aminoacylation, with m-tyr being a more efficient substrate (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation assays shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: G318W PheRS was unable to utilize o-Tyr or L-DOPA for tRNAPhe aminoacylation.
source: Under similar conditions, G318W PheRS was unable to utilize o-Tyr or L-DOPA for tRNAPhe aminoacylation, consistent with the absence of any growth phenotype of the pheT(G318W) strain in the presence of these tyrosine analogs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) for m-Tyr activation by EcPheRS is 35-fold less than for Phe.
source: Examination of amino acid substrate specificity showed the catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) for m-Tyr activation by EcPheRS to be 35-fold less than for Phe, in contrast to p-Tyr which is activated almost 3000-fold less efficiently than the cognate substrate (Table 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic data shown in Table 2.

claim: p-Tyr is activated almost 3000-fold less efficiently than Phe by EcPheRS.
source: Examination of amino acid substrate specificity showed the catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) for m-Tyr activation by EcPheRS to be 35-fold less than for Phe, in contrast to p-Tyr which is activated almost 3000-fold less efficiently than the cognate substrate (Table 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic data shown in Table 2.

claim: Wild type ScctPheRS efficiently utilizes m-Tyr for activation and aminoacylation of tRNAPhe.
source: In contrast to the E. coli enzyme, wild type ScctPheRS efficiently utilizes m-Tyr for activation and aminoacylation of tRNAPhe. Charging of tRNAPhe with m-Tyr was seen at amino acid substrate concentrations where p-Tyr-tRNAPhe synthesis was not detected (Figure 4C; Table 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation assays shown in Figure 4C and kinetic data in Table 2.

claim: The kcat/KM of m-Tyr activation by ScctPheRS is 71-fold lower than that of Phe.
source: The kcat/KM of m-Tyr activation by ScctPheRS is 71-fold lower than that of Phe, demonstrating relatively poor discrimination between the two amino acids (Table 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic data shown in Table 2.

claim: p-Tyr-tRNAPhe is a better substrate for post-transfer editing by ScctPheRS relative to m-Tyr-tRNAPhe.
source: In contrast to the E. coli enzyme, p-Tyr-tRNAPhe is a better substrate for post–transfer editing by ScctPheRS relative to m-Tyr-tRNAPhe (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by editing assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: The mitochondrial variant of yeast PheRS (ScmtPheRS) synthesizes m-Tyr-tRNAPhe more efficiently than p-Tyr-tRNAPhe at similar tyrosine isomer concentrations.
source: The mitochondrial variant of yeast PheRS (ScmtPheRS), which naturally lacks Tyr-tRNAPhe post–transfer editing activity (Roy et al., 2005), was also found to synthesize m-Tyr-tRNAPhe more efficiently than p-Tyr-tRNAPhe at similar tyrosine isomer concentrations (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation assays shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Similar levels of fMet-m-Tyr and fMet-Phe were synthesized in vitro using m-Tyr-tRNAPhe:EF-Tu:GTP as a substrate for decoding of a ribosomal A site Phe (UUC) codon.
source: Dipeptide synthesis was monitored in vitro using m-Tyr-tRNAPhe:EF-Tu:GTP as a substrate for decoding of a ribosomal A site Phe (UUC) codon. Under these conditions similar levels of fMet-m-Tyr and fMet-Phe were synthesized, indicating a lack of discrimination against the non-proteinogenic amino acid at the A-site of E. coli ribosomes (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dipeptide synthesis assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is a lack of discrimination against m-Tyr at the A-site of E. coli ribosomes.
source: Under these conditions similar levels of fMet-m-Tyr and fMet-Phe were synthesized, indicating a lack of discrimination against the non-proteinogenic amino acid at the A-site of E. coli ribosomes (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that similar levels of dipeptides are formed with m-Tyr and Phe.

claim: Comparison of proteome total amino acid levels between wild type and pheT(G318W) strains indicated a level of misincorporation of 1% m-Tyr at Phe codons due to the absence of PheRS editing.
source: Comparison of proteome total amino acid levels between wild type and pheT(G318W) strains indicated a level of misincorporation of 1% m-Tyr at Phe codons due to the absence of PheRS editing (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS-MRM analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In wild type E. coli proteins the fraction of m-Tyr compared to Phe is 0.015, increasing to 0.025 in samples isolated from the pheT(G318W) strain grown in the same conditions.
source: In wild type proteins the fraction of m-Tyr compared to Phe is 0.015, increasing to 0.025 in samples isolated from the pheT(G318W) strain grown in the same conditions.
evidence: This is based on LC-MS/MS-MRM quantification of amino acids in protein hydrolysates.

claim: Post-transfer editing by PheRS provides protection of the E. coli proteome from misincorporation of m-Tyr at Phe codons.
source: This result indicates post–transfer editing by PheRS provides protection of the E. coli proteome from misincorporation of m-Tyr at Phe codons.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased m-Tyr/Phe ratio in editing-deficient strains.

claim: Quantification of p-Tyr relative to Phe in protein samples does not change between the wild type and pheT(G318W) strains.
source: Quantification of p-Tyr relative to Phe in the protein samples isolated from cultures grown in the presence of 0.5 mM p-Tyr does not change between the wild type and pheT(G318W) strains indicating this protein amino acid is not significantly misincorporated at Phe codons, even in the absence of PheRS editing (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS-MRM analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: p-Tyr is not significantly misincorporated at Phe codons, even in the absence of PheRS editing.
source: Quantification of p-Tyr relative to Phe in the protein samples isolated from cultures grown in the presence of 0.5 mM p-Tyr does not change between the wild type and pheT(G318W) strains indicating this protein amino acid is not significantly misincorporated at Phe codons, even in the absence of PheRS editing (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in p-Tyr/Phe ratio between strains.

claim: Aminoacylation of tRNATyr with m-Tyr by E. coli TyrRS was detected in vitro.
source: Aminoacylation of tRNATyr with m-Tyr by E. coli TyrRS was detected in vitro, suggesting this synthetase may provide a route of m-Tyr incorporation even when PheRS editing is active (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: E. coli TyrRS may provide a route of m-Tyr incorporation even when PheRS editing is active.
source: Aminoacylation of tRNATyr with m-Tyr by E. coli TyrRS was detected in vitro, suggesting this synthetase may provide a route of m-Tyr incorporation even when PheRS editing is active (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that TyrRS can charge tRNATyr with m-Tyr.

claim: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated under oxidative stress via the Fenton reaction are capable of catalyzing the conversion of Phe to m-Tyr.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated under oxidative stress via the Fenton reaction are capable of catalyzing the conversion of Phe to m-Tyr, which could potentially threaten the fidelity of protein synthesis in the absence of editing (Maskos et al., 1992; Stadtman and Levine, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on oxidative damage.

claim: m-Tyr accumulated in the intracellular amino acid pools of ROS-treated E. coli cells.
source: LC-MS/MS-MRM analyses showed that m-Tyr accumulated in the intracellular amino acid pools of ROS-treated cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS-MRM analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Significant de novo o-Tyr accumulation was observed following ROS treatment of E. coli cells.
source: In addition to m-Tyr, significant de novo o-Tyr accumulation was also observed following ROS treatment, although this is not expected to pose a threat to translation fidelity as it is not a substrate for PheRS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS-MRM analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: o-Tyr is not expected to pose a threat to translation fidelity as it is not a substrate for PheRS.
source: In addition to m-Tyr, significant de novo o-Tyr accumulation was also observed following ROS treatment, although this is not expected to pose a threat to translation fidelity as it is not a substrate for PheRS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that o-Tyr does not inhibit growth and is not used by PheRS.

claim: E. coli lacking PheRS editing activity showed a reduction in growth relative to wild type when grown in media where ROS exposure increased.
source: E. coli lacking PheRS editing activity showed a reduction in growth relative to wild type when grown in media where ROS exposure increased, consistent with the accumulation of free m-Tyr and its subsequent utilization in protein synthesis (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays under oxidative stress shown in Figure 7B.

claim: PheRS editing activity affords E. coli protection against the co-translational insertion of non-proteinogenic amino acids that accumulate during oxidative stress.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that PheRS editing activity affords E. coli protection against the co-translational insertion of non-proteinogenic amino acids that accumulate during oxidative stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of m-Tyr accumulation under oxidative stress and growth defects in editing-deficient strains.

claim: The fidelity of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases needs to be at or above 1 in 3,000, which is cited as an approximate overall level of error for protein synthesis.
source: It has long been proposed that the fidelity of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases needs to be at or above 1 in 3,000, which is cited as an approximate overall level of error for protein synthesis (Loftfield and Vanderjagt, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a classic study on translation fidelity.

claim: Protection against both p-Tyr and m-Tyr incorporation at Phe codons appears critical in E. coli.
source: Protection against both p-Tyr and m-Tyr incorporation at Phe codons appears critical in E. coli as the PheRS enzyme maintains high active-site selectivity against p-Tyr as well as post–transfer editing activity against m-Tyr-tRNAPhe.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of high specificity and editing activity.

claim: E. coli PheRS requires editing activity to protect the proteome from toxic effects of the non-proteinogenic amino acid m-Tyr.
source: E. coli PheRS requires this editing activity to protect the proteome from toxic effects of the non-proteinogenic amino acid m-Tyr, which is poorly discriminated against by the active site of the enzyme.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth defects and m-Tyr incorporation in editing-deficient strains.

claim: m-Tyr is poorly discriminated against by the active site of E. coli PheRS.
source: E. coli PheRS requires this editing activity to protect the proteome from toxic effects of the non-proteinogenic amino acid m-Tyr, which is poorly discriminated against by the active site of the enzyme.
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic data showing relatively efficient activation of m-Tyr.

claim: Ala294 is primarily responsible for specificity against binding of para-substituted Phe analogs in E. coli PheRS.
source: Ala294 is primarily responsible for specificity against binding of para-substituted Phe analogs, while Gln174 and Glu210 help stabilize the hydroxyl of non-cognate m-Tyr at position 3 of the ring (E. coli numbering) (Klipcan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies.

claim: Gln174 and Glu210 help stabilize the hydroxyl of non-cognate m-Tyr at position 3 of the ring in E. coli PheRS.
source: Ala294 is primarily responsible for specificity against binding of para-substituted Phe analogs, while Gln174 and Glu210 help stabilize the hydroxyl of non-cognate m-Tyr at position 3 of the ring (E. coli numbering) (Klipcan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies.

claim: Glu210 is needed to hydrogen bond with the Phe amino group, ensuring correct orientation of the substrate for activation in E. coli PheRS.
source: In the case of the cognate Phe substrate, Glu210 is also needed to hydrogen bond with the Phe amino group, ensuring correct orientation of the substrate for activation (Safro et al., 2005; Mermershtain et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: It is unlikely E. coli PheRS can select against recognition of m-Tyr while still maintaining efficient activity for the cognate amino acid.
source: It is unlikely this enzyme selects against recognition of m-Tyr while still maintaining efficient activity for the cognate amino acid, therefore the maintenance of post–transfer editing activity is critical for fidelity in E. coli.
evidence: This is inferred from structural and kinetic considerations.

claim: The maintenance of post-transfer editing activity is critical for fidelity in E. coli.
source: It is unlikely this enzyme selects against recognition of m-Tyr while still maintaining efficient activity for the cognate amino acid, therefore the maintenance of post–transfer editing activity is critical for fidelity in E. coli.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to discriminate against m-Tyr at the active site.

claim: In eukaryotes, cytoplasmic PheRS editing is needed to protect the proteome from p-Tyr misincorporation.
source: In eukaryotes, cytoplasmic PheRS editing is needed to protect the proteome from p-Tyr misincorporation. This finding concurs with the low Phe/p-Tyr specificity of the yeast cytoplasmic enzyme (Reynolds et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the p-Tyr sensitivity of editing-deficient yeast strains.

claim: The yeast strain encoding wild type ctPheRS is sensitive to high concentrations of m-Tyr.
source: It is unclear if protection from m-Tyr incorporation is achieved through editing as the yeast strain encoding wild type ctPheRS is sensitive to high concentrations of m-Tyr
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays showing m-Tyr sensitivity in wild-type yeast.

claim: Naturally occurring non-proteinogenic amino acids occur widely in nature and are well-characterized by-products and/or intermediates of biosynthetic pathways.
source: Naturally occurring non-proteinogenic amino acids occur widely in nature and are well-characterized by-products and/or intermediates of biosynthetic pathways (Richmond, 1962).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review on non-proteinogenic amino acids.

claim: The non-proteinogenic amino acid m-Tyr has been detected in several eukaryotic proteomes.
source: The non-proteinogenic amino acid m-Tyr has been detected in several eukaryotic proteomes and is one of the products of canonical aromatic amino acid oxidation (Wells-Knecht et al., 1993; Pennathur et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies detecting m-Tyr in proteomes.

claim: m-Tyr is one of the products of canonical aromatic amino acid oxidation.
source: The non-proteinogenic amino acid m-Tyr has been detected in several eukaryotic proteomes and is one of the products of canonical aromatic amino acid oxidation (Wells-Knecht et al., 1993; Pennathur et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on oxidative damage.

claim: The presence of hydroxylated forms of tyrosine in proteomes has previously been attributed to post-translational damage to proteins by hydroxyl radical species.
source: The presence of hydroxylated forms of tyrosine in proteomes has previously been attributed to post-translational damage to proteins by hydroxyl radical species, and is often used as a marker for tissue damage due to the oxidative conditions of aging and disease.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field of oxidative stress.

claim: m-Tyr and other Tyr analogs are substrates for translation in some organisms and could potentially be incorporated directly during protein synthesis.
source: It has also been shown that m-Tyr and other Tyr analogs, for example L-DOPA, are substrates for translation in some organisms and could potentially be incorporated directly during protein synthesis (Rodgers et al., 2002; Ozawa et al., 2005; Gurer-Orhan et al., 2006; Klipcan et al., 2009; Moor et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on non-proteinogenic amino acid incorporation.

claim: Incorporation of m-Tyr into the proteome of E. coli at Phe codons is toxic to the cell.
source: Incorporation of m-Tyr into the proteome of E. coli at Phe codons is toxic to the cell, and in the absence of PheRS quality control this non-proteinogenic amino acid serves as an efficient substrate for translation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth inhibition and m-Tyr incorporation data.

claim: In the absence of PheRS quality control, m-Tyr serves as an efficient substrate for translation in E. coli.
source: Incorporation of m-Tyr into the proteome of E. coli at Phe codons is toxic to the cell, and in the absence of PheRS quality control this non-proteinogenic amino acid serves as an efficient substrate for translation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation and dipeptide synthesis assays.

claim: α-aminobutyrate in the absence of ValRS editing is toxic at high concentrations.
source: Other non-proteinogenic amino acids have also been shown to be potential threats to translation, such as α-aminobutyrate, which in the absence of ValRS editing is toxic at high concentrations, although the physiological conditions under which this non-protein amino acid might naturally accumulate to significant levels are unclear (Nangle et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on ValRS editing.

claim: The presence of m-Tyr in the proteome of wild type E. coli suggests misincorporation can also occur at Tyr codons but without cytotoxic sequelae.
source: In contrast, the presence of m-Tyr in the proteome of wild type E. coli suggests misincorporation can also occur at Tyr codons but without cytotoxic sequelae.
evidence: This is inferred from the detection of m-Tyr in wild-type proteomes and the lack of growth defects.

claim: The cellular effects of non-proteinogenic amino acid incorporation are codon-dependent.
source: These findings suggest that the cellular effects of non-proteinogenic amino acid incorporation are codon-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential toxicity of m-Tyr at Phe vs Tyr codons.

claim: Misincorporation of m-Tyr at Phe codons in the absence of PheRS quality control occurred at a frequency of 1% and had a significant impact on cellular viability and restricted growth.
source: In E. coli, misincorporation of m-Tyr at Phe codons in the absence of PheRS quality control occurred at a frequency of 1% and had a significant impact on cellular viability and restricted growth.
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS-MRM quantification and growth assays.

claim: Misincorporation of canonical amino acids has been shown to be tolerated at rates of up to 10% without inhibiting growth.
source: This contrasts with the effects of misincorporation of canonical amino acids, which have been shown to be tolerated at rates of up to 10% without inhibiting growth (Ruan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on mistranslation tolerance.

claim: The misincorporation of non-proteinogenic amino acids presents a substantial challenge for protein synthesis quality control.
source: Taken together with earlier studies, our present findings now show that the misincorporation of non-proteinogenic amino acids presents a substantial challenge for protein synthesis quality control.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of toxicity at low misincorporation rates.

claim: Many 'dispensable' editing functions may actually be essential for growth under conditions that lead to the accumulation of potentially toxic levels of non-proteinogenic amino acids.
source: This in turn suggests that many 'dispensable' editing functions, both in aaRSs and trans editing factors, may actually be essential for growth under conditions that lead to the accumulation of potentially toxic levels of non-proteinogenic amino acids.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings that editing is essential under specific stress conditions.

claim: Oxidation of amino acids by reactive species results in limited alteration of amino acid structure, such as the addition of a hydroxyl group, creating potential in vivo substrates for tRNA misacylation.
source: Oxidation of amino acids by reactive species such as hydroxyl radical and superoxide anions results in limited alteration of amino acid structure, such as the addition of a hydroxyl group, creating potential in vivo substrates for tRNA misacylation.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of oxidative damage to amino acids.

claim: L-DOPA and leucine hydroxide have been shown to be incorporated into proteins in mouse cells.
source: These damaged amino acids challenge the protein synthesis machinery, as for example in the case of L-DOPA, and leucine hydroxide, which have been shown to be incorporated into proteins in mouse cells (Rodgers et al., 2002; Ozawa et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on non-proteinogenic amino acid incorporation.

claim: The formation of intracellular m-Tyr in E. coli under physiological conditions is possibly a result of cellular exposure to H2O2.
source: The formation of intracellular m-Tyr in E. coli under physiological conditions is possibly a result of cellular exposure to H2O2.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known chemistry of oxidative damage.

claim: Aerobic respiration results in elevated endogenous levels of H2O2.
source: Aerobic respiration results in elevated endogenous levels of H2O2, but bacterial cells are also exposed to ROS present in their environment.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of cellular metabolism.

claim: Uncharged H2O2 is able to penetrate the cell membrane and accumulate inside cells whenever H2O2 is present in the extracellular habitat.
source: Uncharged H2O2 is able to penetrate the cell membrane and accumulate inside cells whenever H2O2 is present in the extracellular habitat.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of H2O2 permeability.

claim: At physiological pH, H2O2 quickly oxidizes ferrous iron via the Fenton reaction, generating a hydroxyl radical that can react with nearby cellular targets.
source: At physiological pH, H2O2 quickly oxidizes ferrous iron via the Fenton reaction, generating a hydroxyl radical that can react with nearby cellular targets (Rush et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on the Fenton reaction.

claim: Accumulation of toxic levels of m-Tyr in the intracellular pools of E. coli occurs under experimental conditions that promote the formation of hydroxyl radicals.
source: Accumulation of toxic levels of m-Tyr in the intracellular pools of E. coli occurs under experimental conditions that promote the formation of hydroxyl radicals, however this is not the major byproduct of Phe oxidation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS-MRM analysis of ROS-treated cells.

claim: The o-Tyr isomer is the more abundant hydroxylation product under ROS-generating conditions.
source: The o-Tyr isomer is the more abundant hydroxylation product under ROS-generating conditions used here (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS-MRM analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: There is no observed o-Tyr aminoacylation of tRNAPhe by wild type PheRS in vitro.
source: However, there is no observed o-Tyr aminoacylation of tRNAPhe by wild type PheRS in vitro, or inhibition of cell growth, in the presence of this hydroxylated Phe substrate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation and growth assays.

claim: E. coli PheRS has evolved to effectively discriminate against different Tyr isomers using a combination of substrate specificity (o-Tyr, p-Tyr) and editing activity (m-Tyr, p-Tyr).
source: These, and the corresponding biochemical data, indicate how E. coli PheRS has evolved to effectively discriminate against different Tyr isomers using a combination of substrate specificity (o-Tyr, p-Tyr) and editing activity (m-Tyr, p-Tyr).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined biochemical and growth data.

claim: Yeast PheRS has mainly evolved specifically to discriminate for p-Tyr by editing.
source: In contrast, yeast PheRS has mainly evolved specifically to discriminate for p-Tyr by editing, reflecting differences in the factors that drive selection of quality control mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the yeast PheRS specificity and editing data.
